claim: TRNP1 controls proliferation of neural progenitors in mice and ferrets.
source: A good candidate for such a comparative approach is TRNP1, as it controls proliferation of neural progenitors in mice and ferrets.
evidence: Cited as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: The rate of TRNP1 protein evolution (ω) significantly correlates with brain size.
source: We find that the rate of TRNP1 protein evolution (ω) significantly correlates with brain size, slightly less with cortical folding and much less with body size.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by Coevol analysis results

claim: The brain correlation of TRNP1 protein evolution is stronger than for >95% of random control proteins.
source: This brain correlation is stronger than for >95% of random control proteins.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by comparison with 124 control proteins

claim: TRNP1 from species with larger brains and more cortical folding induce higher proliferation rates in neural stem cells.
source: This co-evolution is likely affecting TRNP1 activity, as we find that TRNP1 from species with larger brains and more cortical folding induce higher proliferation rates in neural stem cells.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by proliferation assay data

claim: One CRE of TRNP1 likely co-evolves with cortical folding in Old World monkeys and apes.
source: Furthermore, we compare the activity of putative cis-regulatory elements (CREs) of TRNP1 in a massively parallel reporter assay and identify one CRE that likely co-evolves with cortical folding in Old World monkeys and apes.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by MPRA data

claim: Coding and regulatory changes that increased TRNP1 activity were positively selected either as a cause or a consequence of increases in brain size and cortical folding.
source: Our analyses indicate that coding and regulatory changes that increased TRNP1 activity were positively selected either as a cause or a consequence of increases in brain size and cortical folding.
evidence: Stated as conclusion in abstract based on multiple lines of evidence

claim: Brain size and cortical folding show extensive variation across mammals, including recurrent independent increases and decreases.
source: Brain size and cortical folding show extensive variation across mammals, including recurrent independent increases and decreases (Montgomery et al., 2016; Boddy et al., 2012; Lewitus et al., 2013; Smaers et al., 2021).

claim: Most rodents have a small brain and an unfolded cortex.
source: For example, most rodents have a small brain and an unfolded cortex (Kelava et al., 2013)

claim: Carnivores, cetaceans, and primates generally have enlarged and folded cortices.
source: while carnivores, cetaceans, and primates generally have enlarged and folded cortices, peaking in dolphin and human.
evidence: Stated as general knowledge in introduction

claim: Expressing Trnp1 in neural stem cells isolated from mouse cortices induces phase separation, accelerates mitosis, and increases proliferation.
source: On a cellular level, expressing Trnp1 in neural stem cells (NSCs) isolated from mouse cortices induces phase separation, accelerates mitosis, and increases proliferation (Stahl et al., 2013; Esgleas et al., 2020).

claim: Increasing Trnp1 expression by in utero electroporation in mice and ferrets leads to increased proliferation of aRGCs.
source: Increasing Trnp1 expression by in utero electroporation in mice and ferrets (embryonic day 13 [E13] in mice) leads to increased proliferation of aRGCs (Stahl et al., 2013; Martínez-Martínez et al., 2016).

claim: Decreasing Trnp1 expression levels in mice or ferrets reduces aRGC proliferation, increases their differentiation into BPs, and induces cortical folding.
source: Decreasing Trnp1 expression levels in mice or ferrets (E13) reduces aRGC proliferation, increases their differentiation into BPs, and induces cortical folding (Stahl et al., 2013; Pilz et al., 2013; Martínez-Martínez et al., 2016).

claim: Increasing Trnp1 expression levels by in utero electroporation at E14.5 increases bRGC proliferation and induces cortical folding.
source: Notably, increasing Trnp1 expression levels by in utero electroporation at E14.5 increases bRGC proliferation (Kerimoglu et al., 2021) and also induces cortical folding.

claim: 45 mammalian TRNP1 coding sequences were collected and aligned with 99.0% completeness.
source: We experimentally and computationally collected (Camacho et al., 2009) and aligned (Löytynoja, 2021) 45 mammalian TRNP1 coding sequences, including dolphin and 18 primates (99.0% completeness, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Brain size and cortical folding estimates were compiled for 30 mammalian species.
source: For 30 of those species, we could also compile estimates for brain size and cortical folding, as well as body mass as a potentially confounding parameter (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1c).

claim: ω of TRNP1 positively correlates with brain size (r=0.83; p=0.97).
source: Indeed, we find that ω of TRNP1 positively correlates with brain size (r=0.83; p=0.97), GI (r=0.75; p=0.98), and also body mass (r=0.76; p=0.97)

claim: ω of TRNP1 positively correlates with GI (r=0.75; p=0.98).
source: Indeed, we find that ω of TRNP1 positively correlates with brain size (r=0.83; p=0.97), GI (r=0.75; p=0.98), and also body mass (r=0.76; p=0.97)

claim: ω of TRNP1 positively correlates with body mass (r=0.76; p=0.97).
source: Indeed, we find that ω of TRNP1 positively correlates with brain size (r=0.83; p=0.97), GI (r=0.75; p=0.98), and also body mass (r=0.76; p=0.97)

claim: The correlations of TRNP1 ω with brain size, GI, and body mass are stronger than those of the average control protein.
source: and that these correlations are stronger than those of the average control protein (Figure 1C–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: Comparison with 124 control proteins shown in figures

claim: Brain size has the highest partial correlation with TRNP1 ω (r=0.4).
source: To disentangle which trait is most likely to be causal for the observed correlation with ω, we compare the partial correlations and find that brain size has the highest partial correlation (r=0.4), followed by GI (r=0.34), while the partial correlation with body mass (r=0.19) has a much larger drop compared to the marginals

claim: TRNP1 protein evolution is among 4.0% of the most correlated proteins for brain size.
source: We find that TRNP1 protein evolution is among 4.0% and 6.4% of the most correlated proteins for brain size and GI, respectively.

claim: TRNP1 protein evolution is among 6.4% of the most correlated proteins for GI.
source: We find that TRNP1 protein evolution is among 4.0% and 6.4% of the most correlated proteins for brain size and GI, respectively.

claim: Eight codons in TRNP1 with a selection signature could be pinpointed with high confidence.
source: Eight codons with a selection signature could be pinpointed with high confidence (Supplementary file 1d).

claim: Seven out of eight positively selected codons in TRNP1 reside within the first intrinsically disordered region (IDR).
source: Seven out of those eight reside within the first intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and one in the second IDR of the protein (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The IDRs of TRNP1 are thought to mediate homotypic and heterotypic protein-protein interactions.
source: The IDRs of TRNP1 are thought to mediate homotypic and heterotypic protein-protein interactions and are relevant for TRNP1-dependent phase separation, nuclear compartment size regulation, and M‐phase length regulation (Esgleas et al., 2020).

claim: The proportion of proliferating cells was highest in cells transfected with dolphin TRNP1 followed by human.
source: Remarkably, the proportion of proliferating cells was highest in cells transfected with dolphin TRNP1 followed by human, which was significantly higher than the two other primates, galago and macaque (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 2a-c).

claim: Three upstream CREs, the promoter-including exon 1, an intron CRE, one CRE overlapping the second exon, and one downstream CRE were identified for TRNP1.
source: To identify putative CREs of TRNP1, we used DNase hypersensitive sites (DHS) from human foetal brain (Bernstein et al., 2010) and found three upstream CREs, the promoter-including exon 1, an intron CRE, one CRE overlapping the second exon, and one downstream CRE (Figure 3A).

claim: A total of 351 putative CREs of TRNP1 were obtained in a panel of 75 mammalian species.
source: We obtained the orthologous sequences of the human CREs using a reciprocal best blat (RBB) strategy across additional mammalian species either from genome databases or by sequencing, yielding a total of 351 putative CREs in a panel of 75 mammalian species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The MPRA plasmid library contained at least 4251 (86%) CRE sequence tiles.
source: From those, we constructed a complex and unbiased lentiviral plasmid library containing at least 4251 (86%) CRE sequence tiles (Figure 3B and C).

claim: The CREs covering exon 1, the intron, and the CRE downstream of TRNP1 show the highest total activity across species.
source: The CREs covering exon 1, the intron, and the CRE downstream of TRNP1 show the highest total activity across species while the CREs upstream of TRNP1 show the lowest activity (Figure 3E).

claim: The intron CRE had a tendency to be positively associated with gyrification (PGLS, uncorrected LRT p-value=0.097).
source: None of the CREs showed a significant association with brain size or GI (PGLS, LRT uncorrected p-value > 0.05) and only the intron CRE had a tendency to be positively associated with gyrification (PGLS, uncorrected LRT p-value=0.097, Figure 3F, left; Supplementary file 3b).

claim: When restricted to the catarrhine clade, the association between intron CRE activity and GI becomes considerably stronger (PGLS, uncorrected LRT p-value=0.003, Bonferroni-corrected p-value=0.02).
source: Indeed, when we restrict our analysis to the catarrhine clade that encompasses Old World monkeys, great apes, and humans, the association between intron CRE activity and GI becomes considerably stronger (PGLS, uncorrected LRT p-value=0.003, Bonferroni-corrected for seven regions p-value=0.02, Figure 3F, right; Supplementary file 3).

claim: 8/1000 (0.8%) of random CRE combinations have an association with GI as significant as the intron CRE (p ≤ 0.003).
source: To validate that our model results are rather specific, we generated a null distribution for the observed correlation across catharrines, permuting the activities of all other CREs of this study. In agreement with our model results, we find 8/1000 (0.8%) of the random CRE combinations to have such a significant association of p ≤ 0.003.

claim: Reilly et al. found a gain in enhancer activity on the human lineage in a region overlapping the intron CRE.
source: Furthermore, Reilly et al. compared enhancer activity by histone modifications in the developing cortex of humans, rhesus macaques, and mice and found a gain in activity on the human lineage in a region overlapping the intron CRE (Reilly et al., 2015).

claim: TRNP1 was expressed in the NPC samples used for MPRA.
source: Notably, also TRNP1 was expressed (Figure 4B), supporting the relevance of our cellular system.

claim: TRNP1 expression was significantly higher in human NPC lines than that of cynomolgus macaque's (BH-adjusted p-value <0.05).
source: Moreover, TRNP1 expression was significantly higher in human NPC lines than that of cynomolgus macaque's (BH-adjusted p-value <0.05, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), consistent with higher intron CRE activity.

claim: 22 transcription factors with an excess of binding sites within the catarrhine intron CRE sequences were identified.
source: Among the 392 expressed TFs with known binding motifs, we identified 22 with an excess of binding sites (Frith et al., 2003) within the catarrhine intron CRE sequences (Figure 4B and D).

claim: The 22 TFs with enriched binding sites are enriched in biological processes regulating cell proliferation, neuron apoptotic process, and hormone levels.
source: In agreement with TRNP1 itself being involved in the regulation of cell proliferation (Volpe et al., 2006; Stahl et al., 2013; Esgleas et al., 2020), these 22 TFs are enriched in biological processes regulating cell proliferation, neuron apoptotic process, and hormone levels (Gene Ontology, Fisher's exact p-value <0.05, background: 392 expressed TFs; Figure 4C; Supplementary file 3).

claim: Three TFs (CTCF, ZBTB26, SOX8) are the best candidates to explain the variation in the intron CRE activity.
source: We found three TFs (CTCF, ZBTB26, SOX8) to be the best candidates to explain the variation in the intron CRE activity and one TF (CTCF) to co-vary with GI (PGLS, uncorrected LRT p-value <0.05, Figure 4D–F).
evidence: PGLS modeling of TF binding scores

claim: CTCF binding scores co-vary with GI (PGLS, uncorrected LRT p-value <0.05).
source: We found three TFs (CTCF, ZBTB26, SOX8) to be the best candidates to explain the variation in the intron CRE activity and one TF (CTCF) to co-vary with GI (PGLS, uncorrected LRT p-value <0.05, Figure 4D–F).
evidence: PGLS modeling of TF binding scores

claim: CTCF ChIP-seq data suggests that the CTCF binding site in the intron CRE is bound by CTCF in human NPCs.
source: While the statistical support for this association is not strong, which is expected given that we were screening 22 candidate TFs in only 10 species, CTCF ChIP-seq data from the relevant cell types suggests that this particular CTCF binding site is indeed bound by CTCF in human NPCs (ChiP-seq, Encode Project Consortium, 2012, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: HiC data show a topologically associated domain (TAD) boundary just upstream of TRNP1 in the germinal zone of the developing human brain.
source: Moreover, HiC data show a topologically associated domain (TAD) boundary just upstream of TRNP1 in the germinal zone of the developing human brain (postconception week 8, Won et al., 2016).

claim: The rate of protein evolution and the proliferative activity of TRNP1 positively correlate with brain size and gyrification in mammals.
source: We applied phylogenetic methods to explore associations between sequence and trait evolution and found that the rate of protein evolution and the proliferative activity of TRNP1 positively correlate with brain size and gyrification in mammals.

claim: Body size correlates much less with TRNP1 protein evolution than brain size or gyrification.
source: However, body size – a reasonable proxy for effective population size (Figuet et al., 2016; Lartillot and Poujol, 2011) – correlates much less with TRNP1 protein evolution than brain size or gyrification.
evidence: Comparison of correlation strengths from Coevol analysis

claim: The correlation of TRNP1 with brain size and gyrification is much stronger than the average correlation of these traits with the evolution of other proteins.
source: Even more convincingly, the correlation of TRNP1 with brain size and gyrification is much stronger than the average correlation of these traits with the evolution of other proteins, that would have had to experience the same population size changes.

claim: The observed correlations are best interpreted as co-evolution of TRNP1 activity with brain size and gyrification.
source: Together with the known role of TRNP1 in brain development, we think that the observed correlations are best interpreted as co-evolution of TRNP1 activity with brain size and gyrification, that is, that more active TRNP1 alleles were selected because they were advantageous to increase brain size and/or gyrification.

claim: The effect of structural changes in TRNP1 appears stronger than the effect of regulatory changes.
source: Of note, the effect of structural changes appears stronger than the effect of regulatory changes.
evidence: Comparison of correlation strengths in discussion

claim: Current measures of regulatory activity are inherently less precise than counting amino acid changes.
source: However, current measures of regulatory activity are inherently less precise than counting amino acid changes, which will necessarily deflate the estimated association strength (Danko et al., 2018; Berthelot et al., 2018; Huber et al., 2020).

claim: INSM1 controls NEC-to-neural-progenitor transition.
source: These include INSM1 (Tavano et al., 2018), which also has been shown to control NEC-to-neural-progenitor transition

claim: TFAP2A, NFIC, TCF3, KLF12, and INSM1 have increased activity in human neural stem and progenitor cells during early cortical development compared to later stages.
source: as well as other relevant factors with increased activity in human neural stem and progenitor cells during early cortical development compared to later stages, such as TFAP2A, NFIC, TCF3, KLF12, and again INSM1 (Trevino et al., 2021; de la Torre-Ubieta et al., 2018).

claim: CTCF can act as transcriptional activator and recruit co-factors in a lineage-specific manner.
source: Although CTCF is best known for its insulating properties, it can also act as transcriptional activator and recruit co-factors in a lineage-specific manner (Arzate-Mejía et al., 2018).

claim: In neural progenitors, CTCF loss causes severe impairment in proliferative capacity through the increase in premature cell cycle exit.
source: In neural progenitors, CTCF loss causes severe impairment in proliferative capacity through the increase in premature cell cycle exit, which results in drastically reduced progenitor pool and early differentiation (Watson et al., 2014).

claim: When overexpressing Trnp1 in aRGCs of developing mice (E13) and ferrets (E30), aRGC proliferation increases.
source: When overexpressing Trnp1 in aRGCs of developing mice (E13) and ferrets (E30), aRGC proliferation increases (Stahl et al., 2013; Pilz et al., 2013; Martínez-Martínez et al., 2016).

claim: Overexpression of Trnp1 increases proliferation in vitro in NSCs or breast cancer cells.
source: Similarly, overexpression of Trnp1 increases proliferation in vitro in NSCs (Stahl et al., 2013; Esgleas et al., 2020) or breast cancer cells (Volpe et al., 2006).

claim: Increases in brain size and especially increases in cortical folding are highly dependent on increases in proliferation of BPs, in particular bRGCs.
source: In addition, increases in brain size and especially increases in cortical folding are highly dependent on increases in proliferation of BPs, in particular bRGCs (Pinson and Huttner, 2021; Del-Valle-Anton and Borrell, 2022; Villalba et al., 2021).

claim: In contrast to non-proliferating BPs from mice, proliferating BPs from human do express TRNP1.
source: Firstly, in contrast to non-proliferating BPs from mice, proliferating BPs from human do express TRNP1 (Kerimoglu et al., 2021).

claim: When activating expression of Trnp1 using CRISPRa at E14.5, more proliferating BPs and induction of cortical folding is observed.
source: Furthermore, when activating expression of Trnp1 using CRISPRa at E14.5, more proliferating BPs and induction of cortical folding is observed (Kerimoglu et al., 2021).

claim: A more active TRNP1 can increase proliferation in aRGCs and BPs and this could cause the observed co-evolution with brain size and cortical folding.
source: Hence, a more active TRNP1 can increase proliferation in aRGCs and BPs and this could cause the observed co-evolution with brain size and cortical folding.
evidence: Inference from cited evidence and current study results

claim: TRNP1 is the first case where analyses of protein sequence, regulatory activity, and protein activity across a larger phylogeny have been combined to investigate the role of a candidate gene in brain evolution.
source: TRNP1 is the first case where analyses of protein sequence, regulatory activity, and protein activity across a larger phylogeny have been combined to investigate the role of a candidate gene in brain evolution.

claim: Proliferation of bRGCs at a particular cortical location is thought to be crucial to generate a cortical fold at this location.
source: Notably, proliferation of bRGCs at a particular cortical location is thought to be crucial to generate a cortical fold at this location.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in introduction

claim: The human-specific gene ARHGAP11B was found to induce bRGC proliferation and folding in cortices of mice, ferrets, and marmosets.
source: For example, the human-specific gene ARHGAP11B was found to induce bRGC proliferation and folding in cortices of mice, ferrets, and marmosets (Florio et al., 2015; Kalebic et al., 2018; Heide et al., 2020).

claim: An amino acid substitution specific to modern humans in TKTL1 affects brain development.
source: Other examples include an amino acid substitution specific to modern humans in TKTL1 (Pinson et al., 2022)

claim: Human-specific NOTCH2 paralogs affect brain development.
source: human-specific NOTCH2 paralogs (Fiddes et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2018)

claim: The primate-specific genes TMEM14B and TBC1D3 affect brain development.
source: the primate-specific genes TMEM14B and TBC1D3 (Liu et al., 2017; Ju et al., 2016)

claim: An enhancer of FZD8, a receptor of the Wnt pathway, affects brain development.
source: and an enhancer of FZD8, a receptor of the Wnt pathway (Boyd et al., 2015).

claim: Proliferation of neuroepithelial stem cells (NECs) that have contacts with the apical surface and basal lamina leads to the formation of the neuroepithelium during early development.
source: Briefly, proliferation of neuroepithelial stem cells (NECs) that have contacts with the apical surface and basal lamina leads to the formation of the neuroepithelium during early development.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in introduction

claim: NECs become Pax6-positive apical radial glia cells (aRGCs), that continue to self-amplify before producing basal progenitors (BPs).
source: NECs then become Pax6-positive apical radial glia cells (aRGCs), that continue to self-amplify before producing basal progenitors (BPs).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in introduction

claim: BPs include basal radial glia cells (bRGCs) that remain Pax6 positive, loose the apical contact, and can self-amplify before eventually producing neurons.
source: BPs include basal radial glia cells (bRGCs) that remain Pax6 positive, loose the apical contact, and – depending on the species – can also self-amplify before eventually producing neurons.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in introduction

claim: A short cell cycle leads to more cycles of symmetric divisions, a delayed onset of neurogenesis, and subsequently to more neurons and a bigger cortex.
source: The extent of proliferation of all these neural progenitors is also influenced by their cell cycle length where a short cell cycle leads to more cycles of symmetric divisions, a delayed onset of neurogenesis, and subsequently to more neurons and a bigger cortex.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in introduction
